newsitem.title: GREECE: FOCUS - Athens bourse shaken by settlement mess.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Athens bourse shaken by settlement mess.

text.p: Brokerages stopped all trade at the Athens bourse on Friday after the exchange clearing house failed to pay cash settlements to several brokers on Thursday.
Brokers said the clearing house appeared to have been hit by problems with a member firm's settlement payment of 1.2 billion drachmas ($5.03 million) which had caused a liquidity crunch.
With the equity market's credibility at stake, brokers agreed to halt all trading and not execute orders through their screen-based terminals.
Brokers said they were concerned that other transactions could go unpaid by the clearing house unless the matter was sorted out quickly.

The bourse's problems prompted President Manolis Xanthakis to rush back from a conference in Hong Kong. Brokers association officials were also planning to meet National Economy Minister Yannos Papandoniou to sort out the mess, sources said.
Government spokesman Dimitris Reppas said the bourse must sort out its own problems, however, and ruled out any initiatives by the socialist government elected in September.
"The stock exchange, on its own, will face this problem and everything will go well," he said.
Following morning news headlines of "Shaky Bourse Foundations", the Athens state prosecutor's office ordered an urgent investigation into the settlement mess at the exchange.
The prosecutor's office said another investigation target was a securities company said to have set off the crisis with problems over its payment to the clearing house.
Neither the clearing house nor the securities company has made any comment.

Member firms were demanding government intervention and guarantees on clearing, fearing that if they resumed trade more settlement problems could be encountered. They also demanded payment on executed sell orders due to them from the clearing house.

"Instead of intervening fast to cover the cash problem that erupted, of a relatively small magnitude, and allow the system to keep on going, the government is being indecisive. This could grow into a big problem," a leading broker said.
Market analysts expressed concerns about the problems triggering a domino effect, fearing more brokers might be overstretched on margin and short positions.

"The exchange authorities have been getting a lot more stringent with brokers on compliance issues. If the exchange presses too much some may have to declare bankruptcy," said ING Barings analyst Yannis Protopapadakis.
The clampdown may have opened a pandora's box of problems but, in the long run, it could make for a better market, others said.
Conservative opposition spokesman Prokopis Pavlopoulos blamed the government and Papandoniou, charging they should take full responsibility for the lack of investor protection.
Meanwhile, the bourse problems left shareholders confused and wondering whether trading would resume on Monday.
